message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This proposal is built on our own trading history, not just competitor benchmarking, and that is what makes me confident in it. The key question with any rate rise is price sensitivity, and we have a direct test: when we raised the weekend rate by £10 last June, weekend occupancy went up, from 81% to 89%, the following month. Combined with a value-for-money score of 8.4, the best in our set, and rates £20 to £35 below competitors, everything points the same way. The revenue estimate is deliberately conservative: it assumes no occupancy gain and puts no value at all on the extra Friday and Sunday nights that the two-night minimum will generate, so £204,000 is a floor rather than a target. We have also built in a clear monitoring trigger, so if occupancy does dip we will see it within a month and can respond. Corporate and group commitments are protected. I think this is a well-evidenced, low-risk change that brings our pricing into line with the quality of the hotel.
</author>

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
## What the author says the proposal shows

1. A direct test of price sensitivity: weekend occupancy rose from 81% to 89% after the £10 rise last June.
2. A best-in-set value-for-money score of 8.4 and rates £20–35 below competitors, so everything points the same way.
3. £204,000 is a floor, because it assumes no occupancy gain and no value from the two-night minimum.
4. A monitoring trigger that will catch any dip within a month.
5. Corporate and group commitments are protected.

The core idea is reasonable. A rate of £165 only matches the cheapest hotel in the competitive set, and the value score suggests some headroom. But the proposal's own data undercut its three load-bearing claims:

- The "direct test" is confounded by the hotel's peak season.
- The £204,000 uses the wrong room count and assumes every room is sold at the full public rate.
- The two-night minimum would hit the hotel's largest single Saturday segment, wedding guests, who by the paper's own description stay one night.

## Checks

- **Average occupancy:** the twelve months in Table 1 average 79.2%. Correct.
- **Revenue arithmetic:** 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 = £203,760. The multiplication is correct, but the room count is wrong.
- **Competitor rates:** £145 sits £20–35 below the set's £165–180. Correct.

## Major issues

**1. The price "test" is a seasonal effect.**
The rate went up in the last week of June. July then came in at 89%, against 81% in June. But Section 2 itself says July and August are the strongest months, "driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays", and August reached 93% at the same rate. A June-to-July rise would be expected whatever the price.

The comparison that would actually test sensitivity is July 2025 against July 2024, or the June-to-July change in 2025 against the same change in earlier years. As it stands, the data don't show that guests are insensitive to price. They don't show the opposite either.

**2. The hotel has 112 rooms, not 124.**
Section 2 says 112 rooms; Section 5 uses 124. At 112 rooms, the same calculation gives about **£184,000**.

**3. The £20 doesn't apply to every room sold.**
The calculation applies the rise to every occupied weekend room, but:
- Corporate and group rates are excluded (Section 6).
- Wedding blocks, about 38% of Saturday bookings, normally book at group rates.
- Rooms sold through online travel agencies pay commission on the rate.
- If the BAR includes VAT, as UK consumer room rates usually do, £20 on the rate is about £16.67 to the hotel.

**Illustration:** take 112 rooms, assume wedding blocks are excluded on Saturdays, and allow for VAT. That gives roughly £120,000–150,000 a year before commission. The true figure depends on the BAR share of the room mix, which the paper should report.

**4. The two-night minimum works against the wedding business.**
Section 4 says wedding guests make up about 38% of Saturday bookings and "arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning". A two-night minimum will mostly push these guests to book two nights they don't want, or to stay somewhere else. It may also strain the relationship with Quayside Hall.

The minimum also cuts the other way on the 21 Saturdays that didn't sell out. On those nights there's spare capacity, and a minimum stay turns away single-night bookings that would have filled it. Leaving the minimum unvalued is therefore not "conservative", as the author says. Its effect could be negative.

**5. £204,000 is not a floor.**
The figure assumes:
- the wrong room count;
- every room at the full public rate;
- no VAT or commission;
- no loss of occupancy despite a 14% price rise;
- no loss from the minimum stay.

Most of these push the true figure down, not up. The paper's own wording ("assumed weekend occupancy is maintained") is an assumption, not a floor.

## Points that hold

- **There is room to reprice.** At £165 the hotel would match the cheapest competitor, not exceed the set. Combined with the 8.4 value score, that's a reasonable case.
- **The monitoring plan is sensible.** Weekly pick-up reviews plus a 5-point trigger is a reasonable design.
  - At £165 against £145, BAR room revenue only falls if occupancy drops by more than about 12%, from 79% to about 69%.
  - That makes a 5-point trigger a fair early warning.
  - Two caveats: a monthly trigger reacts slowly, and lost occupancy also means lost food and drink revenue.

## Settled and open

**Settled by the paper's own data:**
- The June-to-July rise coincides with the peak season, so it can't show price insensitivity.
- The room count is inconsistent: 112 in Section 2, 124 in Section 5.
- The revenue estimate applies the £20 to rooms that won't pay it.
- About 38% of Saturday bookings are single-night wedding stays, the segment the minimum stay would hit directly.

**Open, with what would settle each:**

| Question | What would settle it |
|---|---|
| How price-sensitive weekend guests are | Year-on-year July and August occupancy, and booking pace in the weeks after the 2025 rise |
| BAR share of weekend rooms | The room-mix report (BAR, corporate, group, OTA) |
| Whether the BAR includes VAT | The rate set-up in the channel manager |
| Whether 2026 wedding blocks are already contracted | The group bookings diary |
| The effect of the minimum stay on non-sellout Saturdays | Historical length-of-stay data for those nights |

## Recommendation

Approve the £165 weekend BAR with a corrected revenue estimate: 112 rooms, BAR-only, net of VAT, given as a range. Keep the monitoring plan.

**Don't approve a blanket two-night minimum.** If it's tried at all, exclude wedding and group blocks and apply it only to Saturdays forecast to sell out, where it can actually improve revenue.

Replace the "direct test" in Section 3 with a year-on-year comparison, or describe the evidence as competitor positioning and the value score alone.
